# A common minimizing cap at same-parity proper fibers

This exact example has four integer coordinates and one continuous
coordinate. It disproves a proposed lattice restriction on effective
section barycenters, even with traces obtained from actual nearby cap
gradients. It also disproves strict intermediate-integer depth
interpolation at arbitrary positive depth levels, including levels
strictly below the OC target. The points are explicitly **not global
depth maximizers**, so that additional hypothesis is not refuted.

## 1. An actual convex body and exact fibers

For any `T>=1`, put

\[
 C_T=\{(z,x)\in\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R:
       |z_i|\le2\ (i=1,2,3,4),\quad
       \|z\|_\infty-2\le x\le T\}.
                                                               \tag{1}
\]

This is a bounded full-dimensional convex polytope: its lower graph is
the convex function `max_i(|z_i|-2)`, and its upper graph is constant.
Its positive integer fibers are precisely

`K_z=[||z||_infinity-2,T]`, `z in Z={-2,-1,0,1,2}^4`.

All 625 such fibers have positive length. Consider the nonvertical
closed cap and its boundary

`H={x<=0}`, `P={x=0}`.

There are 81 **proper** section indices

`I={-1,0,1}^4`.

Each proper cut has compulsory coarea weight one, since the section
measure is H_0 and the continuous normal has absolute value one. At
the other 544 indices, denoted J, the lower endpoint of K_z is zero.
These supporting sections have full H_0 measure one and an effective
trace between zero and one. No zero-volume original fiber is used.

The real projection of the entire section is the cube `[-2,2]^4`.
Its real proper-index set is exactly the cube's interior; the optional
sections occur only on its boundary. Thus the underlying real section
weight is constant on a convex set, not an arbitrary sampled array.

The mixed measure decomposes, up to null horizontal boundaries, into
three exact product layers:

\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c}
 x\text{-interval}&\text{integer bases}&\text{mass}\\\hline
 [-2,-1]&\{0\}&1\\
 [-1,0]&\{-1,0,1\}^4&81\\
 [0,T]&\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}^4&625T.
 \end{array}                                                  \tag{2}
\]

Consequently

`M_T=82+625T`, `mu_T(H)=82`.                                  (3)

The same-parity integer points `j_+=e_1`, `j_-=-e_1` are proper
indices. Their continuous points `y_+=(e_1,0)`, `y_-=(-e_1,0)`
belong to the interiors of the fibers `[-1,T]`.

## 2. Explicit effective traces and their barycenters

For `j=e_1`, give each proper index weight one. At supporting indices
choose the following trace:

\[
 \theta_z=
 \begin{cases}
 375/397,&z_1=2,\\
 1/2,&z_1=1,\\
 22/397,&z_1\le0.
 \end{cases}                                                  \tag{4}
\]

At a fixed outer slice `z_1=+-2` there are 125 supporting indices.
At each slice `z_1=-1,0,1` there are `125-27=98` supporting indices.
All remaining coordinate moments vanish by coordinate reflections.
The proper indices have total weight 81 and zero first moment. Direct
summation of (4) gives

\[
 \sum_{z\in J}\theta_z=\frac{73390}{397},\qquad
 \sum_{z\in J}z_1\theta_z=\frac{105547}{397}.
\]

Thus the total effective section weight and its first-coordinate
moment are both `105547/397`, and

\[
 \frac{\sum_{z\in I}z+\sum_{z\in J}\theta_z z}
      {81+\sum_{z\in J}\theta_z}=e_1.                       \tag{5}
\]

Reflection of the traces across `z_1=0` gives the barycenter -e_1.
These distinct proper integer indices have the same parity. Coordinate
permutations yield every +-e_i. Their effective total weights are equal,
so convex combinations of these trace arrays give every point of the
crosspolytope `conv{+-e_i:i=1,2,3,4}` as an effective barycenter.

## 3. The traces come from consistent nearby cap gradients

They are not merely independently chosen formal endpoint weights.
At y=(e_1,0), parametrize nearby downward through-point caps by

`H(a)={x<=a.(z-e_1)}`, `a in R^4`.

At a differentiability point sufficiently close to zero, the gradient
of its mixed cap mass is

`sum_(z in I)(z-e_1)
 +sum_(z in J: a.(z-e_1)>0)(z-e_1)`.

Proper fibers stay properly cut. A supporting lower endpoint contributes
its full trace if the threshold enters that fiber, and zero otherwise.
Choose `q=(1,10,100)` in the last three base coordinates. No nonzero
vector in `{-2,-1,0,1,2}^3` has q-dot-product zero: the highest nonzero
base-ten digit dominates all lower digits. For sufficiently small
`epsilon>0`, the two normals

`a_+=(1,epsilon q)`, `a_-=(1,-epsilon q)`

are positive on all supporting `z_1=2`, negative on all `z_1<=0`,
and give complementary nonzero signs on the supporting `z_1=1` slice.
For instance `epsilon=1/1000` works, since `|q.z'|<=222`.
Approach zero along positive multiples of these normals. Averaging
their two gradient limits gives boundary trace

`theta^+=1` on `z_1=2`, `theta^+=0` on `z_1<=0`,
and `theta^+=1/2` on `z_1=1`.

The opposite two normals give the complementary trace `theta^-`.
Including the compulsory proper sections, the first coordinate of the
two average gradients is respectively

`125-81=44`, and `-669-81=-750`.

Every other coordinate is zero. Mixing these two limiting gradients
with weights `375/397` and `22/397` gives zero and exactly (4).
Equivalently (4) is produced by a convex combination of four actual
nearby differentiability gradients, with coefficients
`375/794,375/794,11/397,11/397`.

Thus it is a consistent generalized-gradient certificate for normal
stationarity at the actual through-point cap, not a relaxation that
independently selects incompatible endpoint signs.

It even gives a strict local minimum. In a sufficiently small
neighborhood of a=0, the cap mass equals

`82+sum_(z in I)a.(z-e_1)
    +sum_(z in J)(a.(z-e_1))_+`.

Use (5) to subtract the zero linear form with coefficients theta_z.
Since all traces in (4) lie between `22/397` and `375/397`,

\[
 \mu_T(H(a))-82
 \ge\frac{22}{397}\sum_{z\in J}|a\cdot(z-e_1)|>0
 \quad\text{for }a\ne0.                                   \tag{6}
\]

The last inequality holds because these boundary vectors span R^4.
The next section strengthens this to a global minimum over all normal
directions.

## 4. Every downward cap has mass at least 82

First take T=1 and write `phi(t)=min(1,max(0,t))`. For a downward cap
H(a) at y=(e_1,0), decomposition (2) gives the exact identity

\[
 F(a):=\mu_1(H(a))=82+G(a)-L(a)-\phi(a_1-1),              \tag{7}
\]

where

`G(a)=sum_(z in {-2,...,2}^4) phi(a.z-a_1)`,
`L(a)=sum_(z in {-1,0,1}^4) phi(a_1-a.z)`.

The terms are respectively gain in the positive layer, loss from the
unit negative layer, and loss from the bottom interval at base zero.
Put `A=max_i |a_i|`.

### Gain bound

\[
                         G(a)\ge125\phi(A).                 \tag{8}
\]

For A>0, choose a coordinate having coefficient of absolute value A,
and reflect that coordinate's five values if necessary to make its
coefficient positive. Denote the remaining contribution by Y. Since
`a_1<=A`, the two coordinate levels 2 and 1 alone contribute at least

`sum_Y [phi(A+Y)+phi(Y)]`.

There are 125 remaining-coordinate choices and they are symmetric
under Y -> -Y. For every real t and A>=0,

`phi(A+t)+phi(-t)>=phi(A)`.

If t>=0 or t<=-A, one summand alone proves this; otherwise both
arguments are nonnegative and their sum is A, and clipping at one
cannot make the sum of their clipped values smaller than phi(A).
Summing proves (8). At A=0 it is immediate.

### Loss bound

\[
                  L(a)\le\min(81,102A)\le102\phi(A).        \tag{9}
\]

The first bound 81 is immediate. Replacing each clipped term by its
positive part gives a convex positively homogeneous function of a.
Its maximum on the coefficient cube `[-1,1]^4` occurs at a vertex:
successively express each coordinate as a convex combination of its
two endpoint values. For a vertex with a_1=1, coordinate reflections
show that the sum is always

`sum_(z in {-1,0,1}^4) (1-z_1-z_2-z_3-z_4)_+=102`.

Indeed the multiplicities of the coordinate sum from -4 to 4 are
`1,4,10,16,19,16,10,4,1`, and the contributing weighted sum is
`5+16+30+32+19=102`. At a vertex with a_1=-1, the same symmetry gives
21. Thus the maximum is 102, proving the linear bound in (9).
Its last inequality follows separately for A<=1 and A>=1.

Finally `phi(a_1-1)<=phi(A)`. Equations (7)-(9) give the useful global
estimate

\[
 \boxed{\quad F(a)\ge82+22\min(A,1).\quad}                 \tag{10}
\]

Hence x<=0 is the unique minimizing downward cap direction at this
point. For T>=1, the body only gains source mass in the region x>0;
therefore every fixed downward cap has at least its T=1 mass. Its
mass at a=0 remains 82. This proves the same minimum for every T>=1.

## 5. Upward and vertical caps are strictly larger

For an upward through-point cap `{x>=a.(z-e_1)}`, consider only the
positive product layer. Write `phi_T(t)=min(T,max(0,t))`. Its
contribution is

`sum_(z in {-2,...,2}^4) [T-phi_T(a.z-a_1)]`.

Let `Y=a_2z_2+a_3z_3+a_4z_4`. Use the face z_1=1 and, according
as a_1 is nonnegative or negative, the face z_1=0 or z_1=2.
Their thresholds are Y and `Y-|a_1|`. Pair each remaining-coordinate
vector on the first face with its negative on the second. The two
thresholds then sum to `-|a_1|<=0`, so at most one is positive and

`phi_T(Y)+phi_T(-Y-|a_1|)<=T`.

Each of the 125 pairs contributes at least T to the upward cap. Thus
every upward cap has mass at least `125T>82`.

A vertical through-point halfspace also has mass at least 125T. One
way to retain its positive boundary mass correctly is to approximate
it by upward caps `{x>=-s b.(z-e_1)}`, s increasing to infinity,
if the desired vertical halfspace is `{b.(z-e_1)>=0}`. At bases with
strict sign these caps converge to the corresponding full or empty
fiber; at zero-sign bases they capture only a part of the fiber,
which the closed vertical halfspace contains in full. Consequently
the vertical mass is at least their limiting mass, itself at least
125T. There are finitely many fibers, so this limit is elementary.

Every nonvertical halfspace through the point has one of the two
orientations just considered. Translating any containing halfspace
parallel until it passes through the point can only decrease its
mass. We have therefore proved the exact all-halfspace statement

\[
 \operatorname{depth}_{S_T}(e_1,0)
 =\operatorname{depth}_{S_T}(-e_1,0)
 =\frac{82}{82+625T}.                                      \tag{11}
\]

The reflection equality follows from the symmetry of C_T in each
integer coordinate. The same holds at every (+-e_i,0).

## 6. Consequences, below-target version, and exact limitation

Halfspace depth is quasiconcave: any halfspace containing a convex
combination of points contains at least one of them. Equation (11)
therefore bounds the depth from below by its common value on the
whole crosspolytope `conv{(+-e_i,0):i=1,...,4}`. The single cap x<=0
contains this whole set and has mass 82. Thus depth is exactly the
constant in (11) throughout that crosspolytope, including the proper
integer midpoint `(0,0)` of `(e_1,0)` and `(-e_1,0)`.

This disproves strict positive-level same-parity interpolation in
general integer dimension, and does so even below the OC target.
For the exact rational choice T=5,

\[
 M_5=3207,\qquad
 \frac{82}{3207}<\frac1{32}
       =\frac{\gamma_1}{2^4},
 \qquad 32\cdot82=2624<3207.                               \tag{12}
\]

As T tends to infinity the shared positive depth level tends to zero.
Thus a hypothesis that the common minimizing cap has a small budget,
even strictly below OC, does not repair the proposed interpolation
statement for arbitrary positive-depth points.

The points in (11) are definitely not global maximizers. The point
`(0,T/2)` is the center of the centrally symmetric submeasure
`{-2,...,2}^4 x [0,T]`, whose mass is 625T. Every closed halfspace
containing that point captures at least half that submeasure, including
any boundary mass. The cap x>=T/2 has exactly that mass in the full
source because it excludes the negative layers. Hence

\[
 \operatorname{depth}_{S_T}(0,T/2)
 =\frac{625T}{2(82+625T)}>
   \frac{82}{82+625T}\qquad(T>=1).                         \tag{13}
\]

This establishes the precise scope: the feasible section-barycenter
region and even the level set of a genuinely minimizing common cap
can contain same-parity proper integer points. The construction does
not falsify a theorem restricted to global mixed-depth maximizing
points, and it is not a counterexample to OC.

## 7. Optional higher-continuous-dimensional extension

For any d>=2, take the product of (1) with the centrally symmetric
unit-volume cube `[-1/2,1/2]^(d-1)` in new continuous coordinates w.
The section at x=0 has constant (d-1)-volume one in every base fiber,
and all its continuous first moments are zero. Thus (4)-(5) remain
exact feasible effective section-barycenter certificates.

They remain consistent nearby full-normal certificates, too: the
perturbations above keep the w-normal zero, so their section moment
gradients in w vanish. In a sufficiently small full-normal perturbation
`x<=a.(z-e_1)+b.w`, the excess over 82 equals

`sum_(z in J) integral [(a.(z-e_1)+b.w)_+
                      -theta_z(a.(z-e_1)+b.w)]dw`.

It is bounded below by `22/397` times the corresponding sum of
absolute values. This is positive for every nonzero (a,b): if it
vanished, full-dimensionality of the w cube would force b=0 and the
spanning boundary vectors would force a=0. Therefore the cap is a
strict local minimum in all nonvertical normal parameters for every
d. The global all-halfspace depth assertion (11) was proved for d=1
and is not asserted for these higher-dimensional products.
